title: Automatic Textbook Formalization
claim: System progress shows two distinct phases: steady expansion of output, then a cleanup phase that removes content while preserving the final result.
layout: 2 panels side by side, shared commit x-axis, green/red filled areas
description: Two line-and-area plots share a 'Commit' x-axis running to about 2250. Panel (a), 'Added and removed lines', has a green filled area rising almost linearly to about 180,000 lines. Below the zero line, a red filled area for removed lines grows slowly, then drops sharply near commit 1900 and reaches about -50,000. A legend sits in the top left. Panel (b), 'Lean declarations', shows a green curve rising quickly, then more slowly, to about 6,200 near commit 1900. It then dips and plateaus near 5,900. Both panels use a light green fill under a darker green line. The red removal region in (a) and the dip in (b) mark the cleanup phase. The eye goes first to the large green area on the left.
caption: Progress of the automatic formalization system. Two phases are clearly discernible: continuous code base expansion (including unnecessary rabbit hole content) and cleanup triggered by an update in agent prompts. Each commit represents a separate agent that merges its work into the main branch. At the end, all 340 target theorems and definitions are present and proved.
abstract: We present a case study where an automatic AI system formalizes a textbook with more than 500 pages of graduate-level algebraic combinatorics to Lean. The resulting formalization represents a new milestone in textbook formalization scale and proficiency, moving from early results in undergraduate topology and restructuring of existing library content to a full standalone formalization of a graduate textbook. The formalization comprises 130K lines of code and 5900 Lean declarations and was conducted within one week by a total of 30K Claude 4.5 Opus agents collaborating in parallel on a shared code base via version control, simultaneously setting a record in multi-agent software engineering with usable results. The inference cost matches or undercuts what we estimate as the salaries required for a team of human experts, and we expect there is still the potential for large efficiencies to be made without the need for better models. We make our code, the resulting Lean code base and a side-by-side blueprint website available open-source.
